summary: ADAM (Automated Device for Astronaut Monitoring) is an AI health assistant for astronauts. It combines a smartwatch-style wearable with a hub on the spacecraft to keep track of every crew member’s health around the mission area. Readings from the wearable and the cabin (heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, CO₂, radiation, and more) flow into a time-series database. A deterministic detection layer classifies each indicator as normal, caution, or alert, and an AI assistant named ADAM explains the results in plain language. ADAM also produces daily check-ups, answers crew questions, and draws charts on a live dashboard. Critical alerts are raised on board immediately, while summaries are queued for mission control by priority.
details:
ADAM, your AI Assistant in Space Health

Astronauts have many things in their hands, and most cannot keep tabs on what is most important, their health. Many when they return have various types of health issues, some that could have been prevented if they were aware of them while on their mission.

ADAM, or Automated Device for Astronaut Monitoring, is a combo of a watch-like device and a hub on the spaceship that keeps tabs on all of the crew. It helps them know with daily updates and response to serious health conditions in the moment they happen. The main force behind ADAM is a local-hosted AI LLM that does the check-up on all the crew while also sending the info to control on earth.

  • Fast transmission.
  • Reliabe stability, even in space.
  • Keeps tabs on all the astronauts, at every moment.

How it works:

ADAM works as a loop that runs continuously on board.

  1. Collect: the smartwatch and the cabin sensors send their readings to a hub on the spacecraft, which checks signal quality and stores the raw data.
  2. Detect: a rule-based detection layer, with no AI involved, compares each reading with the astronaut’s normal range and labels it normal, caution, or alert.
  3. Alert or summarize: a critical alert goes straight to the crew on board, without waiting for the AI or for contact with Earth. Routine data goes to the AI assistant.
  4. Explain: the AI assistant turns the data into plain language, produces daily check-ups, answers crew questions, and draws charts on the dashboard.
  5. Report to Earth: messages are queued by priority and sent to mission control. If the link is down, they are held and resent when contact returns.
  6. Review and update: the flight surgeon reviews the data on Earth and can send back signed updates.

Today this is a working prototype running on simulated crew data. The AI assistant still uses a cloud model, and moving it to a model that runs locally on board is the main next step.

How benefits and impact the mission:

Benefits

  • For astronauts: health problems can be caught early instead of after the mission. Daily check-ups and plain-language answers mean less time spent tracking their own health.
  • For mission control: flight surgeons get prioritized summaries instead of raw data, so they can review a whole crew quickly and focus on what matters.
  • For mission planners: critical alerts do not depend on the AI or on contact with Earth, which matters on the Moon (a little over 1 second each way) and on Mars (3 to over 20 minutes each way, plus blackouts).
  • For safety: running the AI assistant locally means the system keeps working during communication loss, and no crew health data leaves the vehicle.

Potential impact

  • It supports a shift from periodic medical checks to continuous monitoring, which long-duration missions will need as help from Earth becomes slower.
  • It shows that AI health tools for space can work without the cloud, with deterministic rules handling alerts and the AI only explaining them.
  • The same design could help in other places with unreliable connectivity, such as remote or isolated medical settings. This is a possible future use, not something we have tested.

Tools and technologies implemented:

  • Languages: Python for the server, simulator, and AI agent. HTML and JavaScript for the dashboard.
  • Software: FastAPI (server and WebSocket ingestion), TimescaleDB (a PostgreSQL time-series database) running in Docker, LangGraph (AI agent with tools), and GitHub for version control.
  • AI model: a DeepSeek language model through its cloud API for now. The code can also point to a local model server such as Ollama, which is our target for running fully on board.
  • Hardware: a simulator generates the crew and cabin data. An ESP32 as set up to send real sensor data to the same server. The full wearable we designed (PPG, ECG, motion, temperature, and more) is a concept described in our hardware report, not a built device.

How is it creative?

  • The AI never decides alerts. A rule-based layer flags problems, and the AI only explains them, so a model error cannot cause a missed alarm.
  • It is built for communication blackouts, not just good connections. Critical alerts work on board, and other messages wait in a priority queue until contact returns.
  • We plan to shrink the AI to the smallest local model that passes our tests, instead of defaulting to the largest one, so it can run on spacecraft hardware.
  • Astronauts talk to their own health data in plain language, and every number the AI gives comes from a database query.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication: ISS coverage gaps, about 1 second of delay each way to the Moon, and 3 to over 20 minutes each way to Mars, plus blackouts.
  • Safety: false alarms and alert fatigue, confirming alerts with two signals, and ADAM supporting the flight surgeon’s decision, not replacing it.
  • Privacy and ethics: a very small crew is easy to identify, so data stays on board, and clinical and research data are kept separate. We also considered the risk of astronauts hiding symptoms if monitoring affected flight eligibility.
  • AI limits: wrong or invented answers, so we plan to check every number in an answer against the database.
  • Hardware limits: power, heat, radiation, and the lack of airflow in microgravity.
  • Standards: NASA crew health, battery, and ISS safety requirements, and space data-link protocols.
  • Honesty about maturity: the prototype uses simulated data and has not been validated on real signals.
Even when things may go array, ADAM will be there to get help as fast as it happens.
